paragraphs.heading: The balance point
paragraphs.text: The center of mass, also called the barycenter or balance point, is the one point where the weighted positions of all the mass in a distribution add up to zero. Borrowing a word from statistics, it is the mean location of the mass. For a system of just two particles it is 𝐑 = (m₁𝐫₁ + m₂𝐫₂)/(m₁ + m₂).

paragraphs.heading: Why it helps
paragraphs.text: For a rigid body, a force applied at the center of mass gives it a linear acceleration with no angular acceleration, so it speeds up without starting to turn. To picture how an object moves, you can imagine all of its mass packed into this single point. Put another way, when you apply Newton's laws of motion, this point acts as a single particle standing in for the whole object. Calculations in mechanics are often simpler when set up around it.

paragraphs.heading: Where it sits
paragraphs.text: In a single rigid body the center of mass stays fixed relative to the body, and if the density is uniform it lies at the centroid. It can even lie outside the body, as it sometimes does for hollow or open shapes such as a horseshoe or a donut. When the mass is split among separate bodies, as with the Solar System's planets, the point may not match the position of any one member.

paragraphs.heading: Planets and frames
paragraphs.text: The center of mass is a handy reference point for the linear and angular momentum of planets and for the motion of rigid bodies. In orbital mechanics, the motion of planets is worked out as if each were a point mass sitting at its center of mass. In what is called the center of mass frame, an inertial frame is chosen so that the system's center of mass stays at rest relative to the origin.

paragraphs.heading: Archimedes and after
paragraphs.text: Nobody knows where the idea came from, but its first known appearance is in the writings of Archimedes of Syracuse in the 3rd century BCE. He showed that weights resting at various points on a lever give the same torque as they would if all of them were moved to one point, their center of mass. In On Floating Bodies he showed that a floating object settles so that its center of mass is as low as it can be. About 50 years after Newton's laws of motion, Leonhard Euler restated Newton's second law in terms of the center of mass.

paragraphs.heading: Mass versus gravity
paragraphs.text: Where gravity can be treated as uniform, the center of mass and the center of gravity are in exactly the same place. A satellite in orbit is different: gravity is slightly stronger on its side nearer the planet, and that difference can create a torque that turns the satellite until its long axis is vertical. In such a case the two centers have to be told apart. Calling the center of mass the center of gravity is a loose habit, but it is common, and when gravity gradient effects are negligible the two are the same.
